chapter: Opinions on singers, promotion and originality
title: White imitators and Scott Hamilton
summary: They discuss subtle promotion of white imitators, with Edison's exchange with a Boston disc jockey about Scott Hamilton and Ben Webster.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Right. You know what I was really getting at was, you know, there is lip service to this idea on the part of whites.

And you get, very subtle sort of promotions of white people who are basically imitators. And you know, there are people who come along. I mean, Django Reinhardt was a very (unintelligible)ort of European.
And, I mean, there were people like Bix Beiderbecke who certainly had something --
That was Lester Young's idol, Frankie Trumbauer.
Yeah. You know, they have something. But at the same time, there is a very sort of subtle kind of prejudice to promote them.

Well, I'll tell you why. It was a cold sort of thing. Now, Frankie Trumbauer's playing would never thrill you like Lester's playing. There was a certain warmth -- it's a certain warmth in the blacks' playing that's like a magnet that will make you -- you know, it's something -- like Scott Hamilton, I had a little set-to with a radio disc jockey in Boston. He was asking me what I thought about Scott Hamilton. I said, for an imitator, he's fantastic. Well, he said, "Well, who?" I said, "Well, if you've heard Ben Webster, you wouldn't have to ask this question." Then he said, "Well, at least can't you give him credit for..." you know. I said, "I don't see how I can." I said, "Instead of me giving him credit and you giving Scott Hamilton credit, why not say the beginning of what he's trying to do was created by Ben Webster." Now, he's getting more introduction to the whole music world than Ben Webster ever had. Ever had.
So why, why, why do that? Why? You should be able to answer that more --

It's a form of white prejudice. There's no question about it. The only thing is, where I find it very hypocritical, here he comes along, now, if I said to one of these people now, I've been playing Ben Webster, Don Byas, Lester Young, Coleman Hawkins records, and I never play Coltrane's records because I can't stand them. Now they will say that I'm living in the past. But the same people, when this kid comes along, and he deserves a lot of credit because he's reviving something that deserves reviving, but the same people that have been saying Ornette Coleman, John Coltrane, they go overboard for this. Now, there's something hypocritical about this.
See, they don't listen. They can't be bothered to listen to Ben Webster on the old records, and so on.
